processing: Young shoots and leaves are sun-dried, or in an older local method dipped in boiling water and then dried in the shade. It stays a simple dried leaf with no tea-style oxidation.
harvest_season: Tender shoots and young leaves are the prized material; a fixed picking calendar is little recorded.
appearance_dry: Plump, rounded, downy buds or thick leaf in brownish red.
appearance_liquor: Bright yellow and clear; stronger brews sold as a cold street drink run darker.
appearance_wet: Thick oval leaves, green on top and pale beneath.
taste_profile: Thick and punchy with a strong camphor aroma, astringent first and then sweet. Newcomers can find the smell odd, and regular drinkers like the bite.

brewing.notes: It is a big-pot drink, usually brewed strong and often served cool in summer. Reduce the leaf if the camphor note is too much at first.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. It is a cheap everyday leaf bought as recent stock, with finer bud-heavy lots costing more; simply keep it dry. The protected name applies to product from six townships in Shimian County.
description:
Laoying cha is a Sichuan summer drink made not from tea but from a Litsea tree in the laurel family. It grows wild and semi-wild across the mountains of Sichuan, and rural households have long gathered their own. In Chengdu and Chongqing it has also been the cheap big-pot cooler of towns and docks.

The process is modest: tender twigs and leaves are sun-dried, and an older method dips them in boiling water and dries them in the shade. One story behind the name comes from this, turning lao yin, scooped and shade-dried, into lao ying, eagle. Another says that only eagles could reach the trees. Both are folk etymology.

The cup is thick and strong: astringent first and then sweet, with a heavy camphor scent. First-timers may not like the smell, and repeat drinkers come back for exactly that kick. Brew it strong in a large pot, and try it cool on a hot day.

The Shimian version is the protected one, and it is praised for full, downy brownish-red buds. Everyday leaf is much coarser. Health promises are common on this tea, so treat them as sales talk.
history:
Chinese accounts link the name to the Compendium of Materia Medica and trace use back as far as the Warring States, with tribute status under the Tang; these local claims are hard to verify. County gazetteers are firmer, with a Republic-era Hanyuan gazetteer naming places around today's Shimian that grew it. Shimian's memorial on the Red Army's 1935 crossing of the Dadu River also displays a copper pot used for it.

On 31 July 2012, Shimian's laoying cha received national geographical indication protection, covering six townships in the county.
